newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major has rejected IRA peace plan, Adams says.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major has rejected IRA peace plan, Adams says.

text.p: Northern Irish republican leader Gerry Adams said on Tuesday he believed British Prime Minister John Major had rejected proposals for a new IRA ceasefire.
Adams, leader of the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein, warned that if he was correct, the republican guerrillas would not resume a 17-month truce they abandoned in February.
"It appears to me that Mr Major is not going to respond in an adequate or a clear way," Adams told reporters in Belfast.
Asked what this meant for a hoped-for renewal of the Irish Republican Army (IRA) ceasefire he said:
"I don't think there is any evidence the IRA is proposing any unilateral initiatives."

Adams and John Hume, leader of the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, had presented Major with a set of conditions for a renewed truce. These included allowing Sinn Fein into talks on the future of Northern Ireland once a truce has been called and dropping demands that the guerrillas disarm before negotiations.

Major has not made any public response, but in parliament on Tuesday he reiterated his call for a "credible" IRA ceasefire and insisted that "IRA terrorism is utterly unacceptable for any purpose, at any time, in any place."
The British government says it is up to the IRA to make the first move.
According to media reports, Hume, who is currently in Belgium, has received an informal response from Major, although his party officials declined to confirm this.
Adams was also vague about his source of information, saying that he was relying "on reports currently floating about."
However, media commentators said it was unlikely that Adams had not seen Major's response and that he was simply issuing a public warning to the British prime minister.
Sinn Fein's chairman Mitchel McLaughlin has already warned Major that he would be making a "lethal miscalculation" if he rejected the proposals.
But pro-British unionist politicians are also warning Major against accepting the proposals.

The Democratic Unionist Party's leader Ian Paisley warned on Thursday that his party could withdraw its vital support for Major's one-seat parliamentary majority if Sinn Fein were granted entry to the talks.
Protestant Loyalist politicians are taking part in the talks because their own guerrillas have stuck to a two-year ceasefire in their battle to keep Northern Ireland under British rule.
